body.heading: Hints are heavy
paragraphs: Many of us ask by hinting — sighing at the washing-up, mentioning how busy we are — and then feel hurt when nobody decodes us. But a hint makes the other person do two jobs: guess the need and meet it.
A direct request is lighter for everyone: “Could you take the bins out tonight?” One sentence, no archaeology required.

body.heading: Ask for the thing, not the verdict
paragraphs: Ask for something specific, small, and doable: a lift on Thursday, an hour of quiet, help with one form. “Support me more” is a verdict nobody knows how to act on; “Come with me on Tuesday” is a plan.
Specific requests can also be refused specifically, which hurts less than a vague rejection of everything you are.

body.heading: Let no be an answer
paragraphs: A real request allows a real no. If only yes is acceptable, it was not a request — it was an instruction wearing a question mark. People can feel the difference, and it changes how safe asking feels for everyone.
When someone says no to your request, thank them for the honesty. You have learned something true, cheaply, and the door stays open for the next ask.

takeaway: Ask plainly, ask specifically, and let the answer be free.
